title: The deepest US lake has no streams flowing in or out
body: Crater Lake in Oregon reaches about 594 metres deep. It fills part of the basin left by Mount Mazama's collapse roughly 7,700 years ago. Precipitation feeds it without a river entering the basin.
takeaway: A lake can be sustained by rain and snow even when its map shows no incoming river.
source: US Geological Survey, Geology and Ecology of Crater Lake National Park
visual: deep still water enclosed by the steep rim of Mount Mazama's caldera

title: Three glaciers shed icebergs into the same Patagonian lake
body: Lake Argentino in southern Argentina stretches roughly 160 km. At its western end, glaciers from the Andes reach the lake system and release icebergs into milky water carrying ground-up rock.
takeaway: Icebergs can form far from the sea wherever a glacier ends in sufficiently deep water.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Los Glaciares National Park
visual: a blue glacier face shedding small blocks of ice into a milky Patagonian lake
